chunks: "The diode gives the inductor current somewhere to go.
When the high-side switch turns off, the inductor current is still flowing, say 2 amps, because an inductor won't let its current jump.
The inductor's voltage is L di over dt , so it will drive its input end, the switch node, to whatever voltage it takes to keep that current going.
The diode, with its anode at ground and cathode at the switch node, turns on as soon as SW falls about 0.
4 volts below ground, and it carries the inductor current while the energy ramps down into the output. If you remove it, nothing on the board provides that path.
The switch node capacitance, a few hundred picofarads, gets the full 2 amps, so SW falls at something like 10 volts per nanosecond until a device breaks over.
That's the FET avalanching, an IC pin's ESD structure conducting, or something failing.
Each cycle you dump a big chunk of the inductor energy, 1 over 2 L I squared , into that device. In my 12 volts to 3.
3 volts example that's about 15 microjoules a cycle, which at 500 kilohertz is several watts in a part that was never sized for it.
The converter will stop regulating and probably die.
In a synchronous bridge the body diode of the low-side FET is already there, so removing an extra Schottky just costs a little efficiency."
